summary: Section 4.1's core holds. With 'not yet back' as the only information, Retain is a one-dimensional stopping problem: keeping is optimal iff nu(a) = (K/L) sup_h F(h|a)/tau(h|a) >= lambda, the first age with nu <= lambda is the earliest optimal drop age, the same test applies at every later age, and the drop set grows with lambda. nu is the Gittins index of the single holding problem and, because every session ages whether held or not, the Whittle index of the session (exact checks on 12 laws x 37 prices, plus Monte Carlo). Three things in 4.1 must change. (1) K must not contain lambda (K_read does): the price-free index is nu = (K0/L)/(g + W - rho), with g = inf_h tau/F, W the queue wait and rho the restore's own hold; it ranks idle prefixes, staged reads and queued turns in one list and does not put staged reads before queued turns as a class. (2) The rising-hazard formula gives 0 whenever there is an end probability (E[R] is infinite, and such a law cannot have a rising hazard), and the falling-hazard formula holds only past the hazard's peak (0.79 s for the tool entry; a myopic hazard rule would evict every lognormal-hinted prefix at its turn's end). (3) 'Evict in increasing nu' is exact only for the priced problem, as a common threshold; under the hard capacity it is exact for exact hints with equal sizes and costs (Belady) and otherwise a heuristic: 2x the optimum in a two-session example, +0.6 to +2.3 % in offline brute force with unequal sizes or costs, and against the priced bound +24 % at 32 sessions, +6 % at 128, +2 to 3 % at 512 to 2,048. For the write (4.2, result 7.3): V_dirty - V_clean - kappa L/beta is the value of writing at some time, not of writing now; at a constant device price writing later weakly dominates writing now, a dirty page has exactly two candidate lives (hold, write, drop; or hold, drop unwritten), and writing at once is optimal when the device is idle or when a forced eviction of the only copy has more than about 0.4 % chance at saturation prices. The draft's cost of a late write, lambda L_p per second, is an upper bound: the rate is L_p (lambda - nu_clean), zero at the due date (1 s late costs 3 to 17 % of lambda L_p); due-date order is optimal for equal-size pages with one convex lateness shape, overdue pages go lowest clean index first with the size cancelling, and the two orders coincide only when index curves do not cross. Eager writing is right on this workload because device time is nearly free at both ends and as insurance, not because 56 to 67 % of positions are read back: that share is the fraction of writes ever needed, which the model reproduces (57 to 74 % for a 30 to 60 s host stay), and a deferred write would skip the rest. Tail-before-head deletion on the SSD is proved when lookups start above the pages concerned and fails when a head stays resident; a shared head's index is a sum over the sessions below it. The mirror's index is (cost of a late backup)/(L x time to GPU eviction): zero if the late copy is asynchronous, but about 6.6 TTFT-seconds per request if it blocks the scheduler at saturation, in which case the eager backup is the optimum. Prices (kappa, c, lambda) were not measured here; every number with them is arithmetic on the brief's constants.

results.name: R1 Holding problem: keep iff nu(a) >= lambda, first passage, dynamic consistency, indexability
results.statement:
Symbols. G in (0, inf] is the gap of one idle period (G = inf: the session never returns). S(t) = P(G > t), p_inf = P(G = inf), I(t) = integral_0^t S(u) du = E[min(G, t)]. At idle age a with S(a) > 0: R = G - a given G > a, F(h|a) = (S(a) - S(a+h))/S(a) = P(R <= h), tau(h|a) = (I(a+h) - I(a))/S(a) = E[min(R, h)]. The prefix has L tokens; holding it costs lambda*L per second (lambda in TTFT-seconds per token-second); if it is dropped before the return and the session returns, K is paid (K >= 0, independent of lambda and of the drop age). The only information over time is 'not yet back'. nu(a) = (K/L) sup_{h>0} F(h|a)/tau(h|a).
Claims. (i) A policy is a drop age s in [a, inf]. Seen from age 0 its cost is C(s) = lambda*L*I(s) + K*(S(s) - p_inf); seen from age a it is (C(s) - lambda*L*I(a))/S(a): every age solves min over s >= a of the same function C. (ii) C(a) - C(a+h) = S(a)*[K*F(h|a) - lambda*L*tau(h|a)]. (iii) Dropping at age a is optimal iff nu(a) <= lambda; keeping is strictly better iff nu(a) > lambda. (iv) s*(a) = min{s >= a : nu(s) <= lambda} exists and is the earliest optimal drop age. (v) Dynamic consistency: at any later age a', reached for whatever reason, the optimal continuation is again 'keep iff nu(a') > lambda'. (vi) Indexability: the drop set D(lambda) = {a : nu(a) <= lambda} grows with lambda; D(0) is the set of ages with no chance of return.
results.proof:
Step 1 (policies). The controller observes only 1{G <= t}. A stopping time of that filtration, even with an independent randomisation U, equals on {G > t} a function s(U) of U alone; after the return nothing is decided. So its cost is E_U[C(s(U))] >= inf_s C(s): deterministic drop ages suffice.
Step 2 (cost). Dropping at s pays rent lambda*L*min(G, s) and pays K iff s < G < inf. Taking expectations, C(s) = lambda*L*I(s) + K*(S(s) - p_inf). Given G > a and s >= a the cost is [lambda*L*(I(s) - I(a)) + K*(S(s) - p_inf)]/S(a) = (C(s) - lambda*L*I(a))/S(a), an increasing affine function of C(s).
Step 3 (difference). C(a) - C(a+h) = K*(S(a) - S(a+h)) - lambda*L*(I(a+h) - I(a)) = S(a)*[K*F(h|a) - lambda*L*tau(h|a)].
Step 4 (test). Dropping at a is optimal iff C(a) <= C(a+h) for all h > 0, iff K*F(h|a) <= lambda*L*tau(h|a) for all h, iff nu(a) <= lambda. If nu(a) > lambda some h has K*F > lambda*L*tau, so keeping until a+h is strictly better.
Step 5 (first passage). S is right-continuous and non-increasing, hence lower semicontinuous; I is continuous; put C(inf) = lim C(s). So C is lower semicontinuous on the compact interval [a, inf] and attains its minimum; let s1 be the smallest minimiser. C(s1) <= C(u) for u >= s1, so nu(s1) <= lambda by Step 4. For a <= s < s1, C(s) > C(s1), so nu(s) > lambda by Step 4. Hence s1 = min{s >= a : nu(s) <= lambda}.
Step 6 (consistency). By Step 2 the problem at any age a' is min over s >= a' of the same C, so the rule at a' does not depend on how a' was reached (Bellman's principle for a deterministic path).
Step 7 (indexability). D(lambda) is defined by nu(a) <= lambda, which is monotone in lambda; nu(a) = 0 iff F(h|a) = 0 for all h.
Ties. At nu(a) = lambda dropping is optimal; keeping until a+h is equally good iff the sup is attained at h. 'Drop at the first age with nu < lambda' is optimal whenever nu falls through lambda without a flat stretch (the falling-hazard case); 'first age with nu <= lambda' is always optimal.

They hold. Two qualifications: at nu = lambda dropping is optimal and keeping is as good only if the sup is attained; and K must be free of lambda (the draft's K_read contains lambda L r; see R7).

results.name: R2 nu is the Gittins index of the holding problem and the Whittle index of the session
results.statement: Let pi(a) = P(G < inf | G > a) and V(a) the optimal priced cost from age a. Then u(a) = K*pi(a) - V(a) = sup over drop ages s >= a of E[K*1{G <= s} - lambda*L*(min(G, s) - a) | G > a]: a process that earns K when it completes (the session returns while the copy is held), is charged lambda*L per second while it runs, and can be retired for 0. The Gittins index of that process (Gittins 1979; the retirement formulation of Whittle 1980: the smallest charge at which retiring is optimal; the fair charge of Weber 1992) is sup_s E[reward]/E[run time] = K*sup_h F(h|a)/tau(h|a) per second, that is nu(a) per token-second. It is the same formula as the index of a job with attained service a in single-server scheduling (Sevcik 1974; Aalto, Ayesta and Righter 2009). Because idle age advances for every session, held or not, and many sessions are held at once, the many-session problem is a restless bandit: nu is the Whittle index (Whittle 1988) of the session's project, and R1 (vi) is Whittle indexability. The Gittins index theorem therefore does not give optimality of the ranking under a hard capacity (see R6).
results.proof: K*pi(a) = K*P(G <= s | G > a) + P(G > s | G > a)*K*pi(s). The policy 'drop at s' costs lambda*L*E[min(G, s) - a | G > a] + P(G > s | G > a)*K*pi(s). Subtracting, K*pi(a) - cost(s) = E[K*1{G <= s} - lambda*L*(min(G, s) - a) | G > a]. Its sup over s is u(a) >= 0, and by R1 u(a) = 0 iff lambda >= nu(a): the charge at which continuing and retiring are equally good is lambda = nu(a), which is the definition of the index in the retirement formulation and of the fair charge sup_s E[K*1{G <= s}]/E[L*(min(G, s) - a)]. Restlessness: the state of a session that is not held (its idle age and hint) keeps moving; Gittins' theorem needs frozen passive arms and one active arm at a time, neither of which holds here. Whittle's index is defined through exactly the priced one-project problem of R1, and indexability is R1 (vi).

results.name: R3 Geometric form: the index is the slope of a convex hull
results.statement: Plot the curve Gamma = {P_t = (I(t), S(t)) : t >= 0}: expected token-seconds held per token against the probability of still being out. Its slope is minus the hazard. (i) (L/K)*nu(a) is minus the slope of the first edge at P_a of the lower convex hull of {P_t : t >= a} (with the limit point (I(inf), p_inf) when I(inf) is finite). (ii) For price lambda the optimal drop age is where a line of slope -lambda*L/K supports that hull. (iii) Falling hazard after a iff Gamma is convex there iff nu = (K/L)*hazard; rising hazard iff concave iff the hull is the chord to the end point. (iv) The lower hull of Gamma is the session's efficient frontier (memory-time per gap against probability of paying K); stretches where the hazard rises are never stopped in. (v) The whole index curve of a law on n points costs O(n) (one monotone-chain pass from the right).
results.proof: C(s) = lambda*L*x + K*y - K*p_inf with (x, y) = P_s is linear with positive weights, so minimising C over s >= a is minimising a linear functional over the curve; minimisers lie on its lower-left convex hull, which gives (ii) and (iv) (mixtures of drop ages give convex combinations). By definition (L/K)*nu(a) = max over s > a of (y_a - y_s)/(x_s - x_a), the steepest descending chord from P_a; P_a is the leftmost point of {P_t : t >= a}, and the first edge of a lower hull from its leftmost point has the smallest slope among all chords from it: (i). dS/dI = -f/S = -hazard, so convexity of Gamma is a falling hazard: (iii). (v) is the standard monotone-chain hull, adding points from right to left.

results.name: R4 Special cases and closed forms (exact hint, falling hazard, rising hazard, ended; Weibull, Lomax, lognormal)
results.statement: eta(t) = f(t)/S(t) is the hazard. (a) Exact hint, return in R0 seconds: nu = K/(L*R0); if the session has ended instead with probability p: nu = K*(1-p)/(L*R0). (b) eta non-increasing on [a, inf) (an end mass is allowed): nu(a) = (K/L)*eta(a+); nu falls with age, the drop set is [a*, inf) (a time-to-live); with one pooled law and equal K/L the order is least recently used. (c) eta non-decreasing on [a, inf) (this forces p_inf = 0): nu(a) = (K/L)/E[R | a], rising with age; the priced problem is decided once, at age 0: keep to the return iff K >= lambda*L*E[G]. (d) Ended session: nu = 0. (e) Any law: nu(a) >= (K/L)*eta(a+), and at an interior best horizon h*, nu(a) = (K/L)*eta(a + h*). (f) Closed forms. Weibull S = exp(-(t/theta)^k): k <= 1: nu = (K/L)*(k/theta)*(a/theta)^(k-1); k >= 1: nu = (K/L)/m(a), m(a) = exp(x)*(theta/k)*Gamma(1/k, x), x = (a/theta)^k (upper incomplete gamma). Lomax S = (1 + t/theta)^(-alpha): nu = (K/L)*alpha/(theta + a), time-to-live a* = alpha*K/(lambda*L) - theta. Lognormal ln G ~ N(m, s^2), z = (ln t - m)/s: eta(t) = phi(z)/(s*t*Phibar(z)), I(t) = t*Phibar(z) + exp(m + s^2/2)*Phi(z - s); the hazard rises up to t* = exp(m + s*z*), z* the root of phi(z)/Phibar(z) = z + s, and falls after; nu(a) = (K/L)*eta(a) for a >= t*; for a < t*, nu(a) = (K/L)*eta(b*) with b* > t* the root of eta(b)*(I(b) - I(a)) = S(a) - S(b).
results.proof: F(h|a)/tau(h|a) = integral_a^{a+h} eta(u) S(u) du / integral_a^{a+h} S(u) du: the S-weighted average of the hazard over [a, a+h] (law with a density on (a, inf) apart from the mass at infinity). (b) If eta is non-increasing the average is non-increasing in h: the sup is the limit h -> 0, eta(a+). (c) If eta is non-decreasing the average is non-decreasing in h: the sup is the limit h -> inf, (S(a) - p_inf)/(I(inf) - I(a)). Since integral_0^inf eta = -ln p_inf, p_inf > 0 would make a non-decreasing eta integrable, hence zero; so p_inf = 0 and the limit is 1/E[R | a]. A rising hazard implies a falling mean residual life, so nu rises. C'(s) = S(s)*(lambda*L - K*eta(s)) changes sign at most once, from + to -, so C is quasi-concave and its minimum is at s = 0 or s = inf: K against lambda*L*E[G]. (a) F(h|a) = 1{h >= R0}, tau = min(h, R0): the ratio is 0 for h < R0 and 1/R0 from R0 on. With an end probability p, for h >= R0: F = 1 - p, tau = (1-p)*R0 + p*h, largest at h = R0. (d) F = 0. (e) the derivative of F/tau in h vanishes iff f_a(h)*tau(h) = F(h)*S_a(h), i.e. eta(a+h) = F(h)/tau(h); the lower bound is the limit h -> 0. (f) Weibull: the hazard (k/theta)(t/theta)^(k-1) is monotone; the mean residual life follows from u = (t/theta)^k. Lomax: hazard alpha/(theta + t). Lognormal: d ln eta/dt = (phi(z)/Phibar(z) - z - s)/(s*t); the inverse Mills ratio minus z falls from inf to 0, so there is one sign change, at z*. I(t) = t*S(t) + integral_0^t u f(u) du, and the partial mean of a lognormal is exp(m + s^2/2)*Phi(z - s). By R3 the curve is concave before t* and convex after, so from a < t* the hull is the tangent from P_a to the convex part; tangency is the stated equation.

results.name: R5 Rising hazard with an end probability: the draft's formula is wrong
results.statement: If P(R < inf) < 1 then E[R] is infinite, so the draft's nu = (K/L)*P(R < inf)/E[R] is 0 for every such law; and no law with P(G = inf) > 0 has a hazard that rises forever. Correct statements. (i) Proper law, rising hazard: nu(a) = (K/L)/E[R | a]. (ii) Sharp hint that may never be honoured: G = inf with probability p, otherwise G0 whose density does not fall on its support, which ends at age b: nu(a) = (K/L)*P(R < inf | a)/E[min(R, b - a) | a]. (iii) In general, with pi(a) = P(the session is alive | idle for a) and F0, tau0 those of the proper part: nu(a) = (K/L)*sup_h pi(a)*F0(h|a)/(pi(a)*tau0(h|a) + (1 - pi(a))*h), with the sup at a finite horizon (possibly h -> 0).
results.proof:
(i) is R4 (c). Impossibility: integral_0^inf eta(t) dt = -ln p_inf is finite when p_inf > 0, and a non-decreasing non-negative integrable function on [0, inf) is zero. (iii) Only live sessions return: F(h|a) = pi(a)*F0(h|a); a dead session is held for the whole horizon: tau(h|a) = pi(a)*tau0(h|a) + (1 - pi(a))*h. As h -> inf the numerator is bounded and the denominator grows linearly, so the ratio tends to 0 and the sup is at a finite h. (ii) The mixture's hazard is (1-p)*f0/(p + (1-p)*S0); on the support the numerator does not fall and the denominator does not rise, so the hazard is non-decreasing up to b and 0 after. The S-weighted average hazard over [a, a+h] (R4) therefore rises up to h = b - a and falls after (only zero-hazard time is added), so the sup is at h = b - a, where F = P(R < inf | a) and tau = E[min(R, b - a) | a].
Counterexample to the draft: G uniform on [15, 25] s with probability 0.9, never with probability 0.1, age 0. True index: 0.9/(0.1*25 + 0.9*20) = 0.0439 K/L per second. Draft: 0.9/inf = 0.

With P(R < inf) = 1 it is right (and 'the longest idle is kept' holds for one pooled law). With an end probability the formula gives 0. Replacement: 'rising hazard (a sharp hint): nu = (K/L)/E[R]; with a chance that the session has ended, nu = (K/L) P(return)/E[min(R, time to the end of the hint's support)]'.

results.name: R6 Many sessions: exact for the priced problem, a heuristic under the hard capacity; the size term
results.statement: Sessions i = 1..N, gaps independent across sessions given the hints, capacity C tokens. Relaxed problem: minimise the long-run restore cost subject to the time-average of held tokens <= C. (i) There is lambda* >= 0 such that 'every session drops its prefix at the first age its index reaches lambda*' (mixing the two tie-breaking versions if needed) is optimal for the relaxed problem; at every instant the prefixes held are those whose index has stayed above lambda* since their turn ended. For every lambda >= 0, sum_i v_i(lambda) - lambda*C (v_i = session i's optimal priced cost rate) is a lower bound on the cost of every non-anticipative policy that respects C at every instant. (ii) Under the hard capacity, 'when full, evict the lowest index' is not optimal in general. Counterexample A (exact hints, one slot, equal sizes): K_A = 1 back in 10 s, K_B = 1.05 back in 11 s; nu_A = 0.100 > nu_B = 0.095, the index evicts B and pays 1.05; evicting A pays 1. Counterexample B (equal sizes and costs, one slot, no early re-fetch): A returns at 1 s with probability 1/2, else never; B returns at 10 s; nu_A = 0.5 K/L > nu_B = 0.1 K/L, the index keeps A and pays K; keeping B pays K/2. (iii) It is exactly optimal for exact hints with equal sizes and equal costs (Belady's rule; Mattson et al. 1970). (iv) Size. The relaxed problem needs no size term beyond K/L. Under the hard capacity the greedy order solves the divisible knapsack and is within one prefix of the integral one. K/L itself depends on L when a read has an exposed fixed lag: K_read/L = c*(V + lags - W)^+/L + (c + kappa)/beta (V the wait in the device's line), so long prefixes go first and one whole prefix goes before the tails of two; with K = mu*gamma*L, or at c = 0, there is no size effect.
results.proof: (i) For any policy p respecting the average constraint and any lambda >= 0: cost(p) >= cost(p) + lambda*(mem(p) - C) >= min over policies of [cost + lambda*mem] - lambda*C = sum_i v_i(lambda) - lambda*C. The minimum separates because the priced objective is a sum over sessions and the other sessions' histories are independent of session i's gap, so they cannot lower session i's priced cost; within a session each gap is a fresh problem solved by R1. v_i is concave in lambda with slope m_i(lambda), the memory used by the index rule (the smallest- and largest-memory optimal rules differ only at ties). Take lambda* with sum m_i(lambda*+) <= C <= sum m_i(lambda*-) (lambda* = 0 if sum m_i(0) <= C) and mix the two tie-breaking rules to meet C: cost = sum v_i(lambda*) - lambda* C, equality in the bound, hence optimal. A policy that respects C at every instant respects it on average, so the bound applies to it. (ii) A: one of the two must go; costs are 1.05 and 1. B: enumeration; the index charges B for 10 s of room at one price although the slot is empty and worthless after 1 s. (iii) Classical. (iv) In the priced problem L multiplies the rent and enters the restore cost only through K, so the comparison of R1 is in K/L; nothing else depends on L. Fractional knapsack: greedy by ratio is optimal for divisible items. Fixed lag: freeing m tokens from one prefix costs P(return)*[c*(V + lags + m/beta - W)^+ + kappa*m/beta]; from two prefixes, m/2 each, the fixed part is paid twice.
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.1 'so keep while nu >= lambda, evict in increasing nu is the exact optimum of the priced single-session problem', 7.2, and 7.10 'Ranking by the index is asymptotically optimal for the relaxed problem as N grows'. 'Keep while nu >= lambda' is exact for the single session; an eviction order is not a single-session object. For the relaxed many-session problem the common threshold is exactly optimal at every N. Ranking is the hard-capacity rule, and it is for the hard-capacity problem that it is asymptotically optimal: for one pooled falling-hazard law this is the time-to-live approximation of LRU (Che et al. 2002; Fricker, Robert and Roberts 2012; Jiang, Nain and Towsley 2018); in general it needs the global-attractor condition of Weber and Weiss (1990), not verified here. Whether LRU is exactly optimal at finite N for one pooled falling-hazard law was not settled.

results.name: R7 Price-free index with the queue: one formula for idle prefixes, staged reads and queued turns
results.statement: A clean prefix of L tokens is in host memory. Its session returns after a remaining gap R (law F(.|a); R = 0 if the turn has arrived) and is admitted W seconds after it returns (W independent of R, mean w): the prefix is next needed on the GPU at T = R + W. If the copy is dropped, the turn restores it at its arrival; this costs K0, free of lambda (K0 = kappa*L/beta + c*E[(r - W)^+], plus p_fail*mu*gamma*L if the re-read can fail; r = wait in the device's line + L/beta + lags), and the restored copy occupies L tokens for rho seconds before admission (the re-read's own hold: from dispatch to admission). Let g(a) = inf_h tau(h|a)/F(h|a), the expected holding time per return over the best horizon: g = 0 for an arrived turn, R0 for an exact hint, 1/hazard for falling hazards, E[R] for rising hazards, inf for an ended session. Claim: keeping (to some horizon, and through the queue once the turn arrives) beats dropping now iff lambda < nu(a) = (K0/L)/(g(a) + w - rho)^+, with nu = inf when g + w <= rho. Special cases. Queued turn: nu_q = [kappa*L/beta + c*E[(r - W)^+]]/(L*(W - rho)^+). Idle prefix, no queue, falling hazard: nu = (K0/L)*eta/(1 - rho*eta) (the paper's eq. retain is this with K0 = rho = r). For equal K0/L, w and rho: nu_staged <= nu_queued, with equality only if g = 0.
results.proof: The policy 'keep until horizon h; if the turn arrives by then keep until admission; otherwise drop and restore at arrival' costs lambda*L*[tau(h|a) + F(h|a)*w] + (P(R < inf | a) - F(h|a))*(K0 + lambda*L*rho). Dropping now costs P(R < inf | a)*(K0 + lambda*L*rho). The difference (drop now minus keep to h) is F(h|a)*K0 - lambda*L*[tau(h|a) + F(h|a)*(w - rho)]. It is positive for some h iff lambda < (K0/L)*sup_h F/(tau + F*(w - rho)) = (K0/L)/(inf_h tau/F + w - rho), since x -> 1/(x + w - rho) is decreasing. This is R1 for the cost function with restore cost K0 + lambda*L*rho and holding time extended by the queue wait, so first passage, consistency and indexability carry over (the drop set {a : nu(a) <= lambda} is monotone in lambda). After arrival g = 0 and the remaining wait only shrinks, so nu_q rises with time: a turn kept at arrival stays kept at a constant price. 'Fits before admission': if r <= W almost surely the numerator is the device price alone; otherwise the stall term enters; if W <= rho nothing is freed and nu = inf.

Differences. (1) K_read contains lambda L r, so 'nu >= lambda' has lambda on both sides; the price-free form moves the read's own hold into the denominator (W_k - rho instead of W_k). Section 6's 'lambda = the index of the marginal holder' is well defined only with this form. (2) A parked read holds no pages (the engine allocates at dispatch), so rho is the time from dispatch to admission, not the whole r. (3) 'Farthest from admission first' holds for equal K0/L. (4) The same formula ranks staged reads (g > 0). 5.1's class order 'staged reads of sessions not yet back, then queued turns' and its scores per token (not per token-second) do not follow from it: at kappa = 1 a queued turn 40 s from admission has nu = 1.2e-6 and yields before a staged read idle 2 s on the tool law with w = 5 s (nu = 5.7e-6). 5.1's staged-read score K_read F_j(r_j | t) presumes a re-staged read; for falling hazards the re-read is at arrival and the stall is (r - W)^+ times P(return). (5) At c = 0 the 'fits' condition is not needed for the sum; it protects the turn's own wait.

results.name: R8 Retain when the dropped prefix can be fetched back early (K replaced by the optimal Fetch cost)
results.statement: Let Phi(a) be the optimal priced cost of a session of idle age a whose prefix is on the SSD only (the value of section 3's Fetch problem, with the read at arrival as recourse), and K' = K0 + lambda*L*rho the cost of a read made at arrival. With early re-fetch the holding problem is V(a) = min(Phi(a), inf_h [lambda*L*tau(h|a) + (1 - F(h|a))*Phi(a+h)]): keeping until a+h beats dropping iff Phi(a) - (1 - F(h|a))*Phi(a+h) > lambda*L*tau(h|a). (i) If the optimal Fetch from every age is 'read at arrival' (falling hazard, or a read hidden by the queue), then Phi(a) = K'*P(return | a) and the test is the index of R7 exactly. (ii) Exact hint R0 whose re-read fits: Phi = kappa*L/beta + lambda*L*rho, and the index is (kappa/beta)/(R0 + W - rho): the order is still farthest next use first, but only device time is at stake; with a free device every prefix whose re-read fits has index 0. (iii) Always Phi(a) - (1 - F(h|a))*Phi(a+h) <= K'*F(h|a): early re-fetch can only lower the value of keeping, so the index with re-fetch is at most the index with K paid at arrival.
results.proof: Structure: after a drop the best continuation is the Fetch problem, so the terminal cost of stopping at age s is Phi(s) instead of K*P(return | s); the rest of R1's argument is unchanged. (i) Phi(a) - (1 - F(h|a))*Phi(a+h) = K'*[P(R < inf | a) - P(h < R < inf | a)] = K'*F(h|a). (ii) Keeping costs lambda*L*(R0 + W); dropping and reading back just in time costs kappa*L/beta + lambda*L*rho; equate. (iii) From age a the policy 'do not read; read at arrival if it comes within h; at a+h follow the optimal Fetch policy' is admissible and costs F(h|a)*K' + (1 - F(h|a))*Phi(a+h) (nothing is held while waiting); Phi(a) is at most that. Monotonicity of the keep set in lambda (indexability with re-fetch) is not proved in general.

Confirmed for falling hazards: the index with K paid at arrival is exact. For sharp hints 4.1's index overstates the value of keeping: the exact-hint bullet 'nu = K/(L R0)' is right only with K = the device price of one read (plus stall if the re-read does not fit), so with a free device a far prefix should be evicted and read back just in time.

results.name: R9 Value of a write; at a constant device price a write is never better early than late
results.statement: Per page of L tokens in host memory at idle age a. Dirty (no complete SSD copy): losing the host copy costs K_d = mu*gamma*L at the return. Clean: K_c = min(K_read, K_d) (restore by the cheaper). A write costs w = kappa*L/beta (plus SSD rent sigma) and is instantaneous here. V0(K; a) = min_s [lambda*L*tau(s-a|a) + K*P(s-a < R < inf | a)] is the optimal cost of one gap with restore cost K and no write. (i) Value of a write against never writing in this gap: D0(a) = V0(K_d; a) - V0(K_c; a) - w = integral_{K_c}^{K_d} P_pay(K; a) dK - w, where P_pay(K; a) is the probability that a page with restore cost K is dropped before the return and the session returns, under its own optimal rule. Hence (K_d - K_c)*P_pay(K_d) <= V0(K_d) - V0(K_c) <= (K_d - K_c)*P_pay(K_c). (ii) D0 > 0 is necessary for the write to be worth making, not sufficient for making it now: for any h such that a clean page would still be held at a+h, 'hold h, then write if the session is not back' costs exactly w*F(h|a) less than 'write now'. With many gaps (the page stays dirty across returns until written or until the session ends) the saving is w*F(h|a)*(1 - q'), q' the probability that the page must be written later anyway; it is still >= 0.
results.proof: (i) V0(K; a) is a minimum over s of functions linear in K, hence concave in K, with derivative P(s*(K) - a < R < inf | a) = P_pay(K; a) wherever the minimiser is unique (envelope theorem); integrate from K_c to K_d. A costlier page is kept longer, so P_pay is non-increasing in K, which gives the two bounds. (ii) Let s_c be the clean drop age and a + h <= s_c. Write now: w + V_c(a) = w + lambda*L*tau(h|a) + (1 - F(h|a))*V_c(a+h), because holding until a+h is optimal for the clean page. Hold h, then write: lambda*L*tau(h|a) + (1 - F(h|a))*(w + V_c(a+h)). The difference is w*F(h|a). With many gaps a return before the write postpones the write with probability q' instead of cancelling it: the saving is w*F*(1 - q').
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.2 'A dirty page has restore cost K_rec, a clean one K_read. The write buys the difference, and only if the host copy goes before the page's next use: value of writing page p now = V_dirty(a) - V_clean(a) - kappa L_p/beta - sigma(...)', and 7.3 'the value of a write'. The sentence is exact (the integral of pay probabilities). The formula is the value of writing at some time. As the value of writing NOW it is wrong: if V_dirty excludes a later write it credits the write made now with a gain a later, cheaper write would also get; if V_dirty includes the later write the expression is <= 0 always and 0 exactly when writing now is optimal. Also K_clean should be min(K_read, K_rec): on an idle FA3 GPU (mu = 1) recompute is the cheaper restore, both values coincide and the write is worth nothing at current prices.

results.name: R10 The two lives of a dirty page; when skipping a write is optimal
results.statement: Model of R9, constant prices. pi(s) = P(G < inf | G > s). From the dirty state the optimal policy is one of two lives: (W) hold until a_w, the first age at which the index with restore cost K_c + w falls to lambda, then write and drop at once; (N) hold until a_d, the first age at which the index with restore cost K_d falls to lambda, then drop unwritten. With C_W(s) = lambda*L*I(s) + (K_c + w)*(S(s) - p_inf) + w*p_inf and C_N(s) = lambda*L*I(s) + K_d*(S(s) - p_inf): V_dirty = min(min_s C_W, min_s C_N), and W is chosen iff V0(K_d) - V0(K_c + w) >= w*p_inf, with V0(K) = min_s [lambda*L*I(s) + K*(S(s) - p_inf)] (from age a: condition on G > a and replace p_inf by 1 - pi(a)). With theta = w/(K_d - K_c): pi(a_w) >= theta is necessary for W and pi(a_d) >= theta is sufficient. Consequences. (1) Ended session (pi = 0): never write; drop at once. (2) No end mass: write iff K_d > K_c + w, per token mu*gamma > K_c/L + kappa/beta. (3) A page that returns before a_w is not written in this gap. (4) Dependence: a larger mu raises K_d (towards W); a larger kappa raises w and K_c (towards N, and a later a_w); a larger lambda makes pages leave younger, when pi is higher (towards W); a law with a long dead tail lowers pi at the drop age (towards N). (5) With a write of duration l_w the write starts at a_w - l_w and is paid with probability S(a_w - l_w) instead of S(a_w).
results.proof: A policy is a pair (u, s): optional write age u <= s and drop age s. If u < s the cost is lambda*L*I(s) + w*S(u) + K_c*(S(s) - p_inf) >= lambda*L*I(s) + w*S(s) + K_c*(S(s) - p_inf), the cost of writing at s: writing strictly before the drop is never better. Without a write the cost is C_N(s). With the write at the drop it is lambda*L*I(s) + (K_c + w)*S(s) - K_c*p_inf = C_W(s). Minimising the lower envelope min(C_W, C_N) over s gives min(min C_W, min C_N). C_W is the holding cost of R1 with restore cost K_c + w plus the constant w*p_inf; C_N is the holding cost with K_d; R1 gives a_w and a_d and the criterion. Thresholds: at a common age s, C_W(s) <= C_N(s) iff w*S(s) <= (K_d - K_c)*(S(s) - p_inf) iff pi(s) >= theta. If W is optimal, C_W(a_w) <= C_N(a_d) <= C_N(a_w), so pi(a_w) >= theta. If pi(a_d) >= theta, min C_W <= C_W(a_d) <= C_N(a_d). (2): p_inf = 0 and V0 is non-decreasing in K.

The last needs a change: the only copy is not kept unconditionally; its index is K_d/K_c times the clean one (86/kappa at saturation) and when it falls to lambda the page is written and dropped, or dropped unwritten if pi < theta. 5.1's 'never dirty pages' contradicts 4.2 for ended sessions: their dirty pages are first out.

results.name: R11 Due date of a write and the cost of missing it
results.statement: Let d_w be the first idle age at which the page's clean index falls to lambda (the age at which a clean copy would be given up). If the page is still dirty and held at age d_w + x, the extra cost of the delay, per second and given the session is not back, is L*(lambda - (K_c/L)*eta(d_w + x)); for falling hazards this is L*(lambda - nu_clean(d_w + x)). It is 0 at the due date, rises with the lateness and tends to lambda*L only as the hazard dies. The cost of being x late is integral_0^x [S(d_w + y)/S(d_w)]*L*(lambda - (K_c/L)*eta(d_w + y)) dy, which is o(x): the due date is soft. Under lazy writing in one gap the page is held to a_w >= d_w (R10); with many gaps the due date lies in [d_w, a_w] and equals d_w when a return only postpones the write.
results.proof: C_c(s) = lambda*L*I(s) + K_c*(S(s) - p_inf) has derivative S(s)*(lambda*L - K_c*eta(s)); holding from d_w to d_w + x instead of dropping at d_w costs C_c(d_w + x) - C_c(d_w), which divided by S(d_w) is the stated integral. For falling hazards nu_clean = (K_c/L)*eta (R4 b) and nu_clean(d_w) = lambda, so the integrand starts at 0. a_w >= d_w because indices are proportional to the restore cost and K_c + w >= K_c. If no clean page can be given up and a read needs the room, the cost is that read's delay (weight c) or a refusal (mu*gamma per token), which is what lambda measures on average.
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.2 'Its write becomes due at d_w = the first time its clean index nu_clean falls below lambda ... Before d_w the write costs only device time; after it every second costs about lambda L_p (room held only because the page is dirty), or a refusal if no clean page is left to give up', and 5.2 'writes are due at d_w and cost lambda L_p per second late'. The definition and the first half hold. The rate lambda L_p is an upper bound reached only for a dead page: the rate is L_p (lambda - nu_clean). So the due date is soft, the Smith ratio of a late write is beta*(lambda - nu_clean) and not beta*lambda, and a late write goes before a late read of L_read tokens iff (lambda - nu_clean)*L_read > c.

results.name: R12 Order of writes on one device
results.statement: (i) Model M1: one device; writes of equal size (one page or one page group, one time slot each, preemption only between pages); page j exists from r_j and has due date d_j; finishing it at C_j costs f(C_j - d_j), with ONE function f for all pages, non-decreasing, convex, zero for x <= 0. Then serving in every slot the released page with the earliest due date (EDD) minimises sum_j f(C_j - d_j), whether or not the due dates can be met. (ii) Feasibility: if some schedule meets every due date, EDD does (Jackson 1955; with release times and preemption, Horn 1974), at zero lateness cost. (iii) Model M3: all pages overdue, sizes L_j, constant cost rates L_j*(lambda - nu_j): the optimal order is by Smith's ratio beta*(lambda - nu_j), lowest clean index first; the size cancels. (iv) 'Lowest clean index first' is the due-date order iff index curves do not cross. With one pooled falling-hazard law and equal K/L both are 'oldest turn end first', the order of a FIFO write queue, and f is convex (its slope L*(lambda - nu_clean) rises). (v) Outside these models (page-specific lateness shapes; unequal sizes with due dates) no order rule is optimal: weighted tardiness on one machine is NP-hard (Lenstra, Rinnooy Kan and Brucker 1977).
results.proof: (i) Exchange. Idling cannot help since f is non-decreasing. Take an optimal non-idling schedule that serves j in the slot ending at t1 while a released page i with d_i < d_j is served in the slot ending at t2 > t1. Swap them (both are released by then). New cost minus old cost = [f(t2 - d_j) - f(t1 - d_j)] - [f(t2 - d_i) - f(t1 - d_i)]. Both brackets are increments of f over an interval of length t2 - t1; the second starts further right (t1 - d_i > t1 - d_j), so by convexity it is at least the first: the swap does not raise the cost. Repeating gives EDD among released pages. (ii) Classical. (iii) Sum of w_j*C_j with w_j = L_j*(lambda - nu_j) and processing time p_j = L_j/beta: Smith's rule orders by w_j/p_j = beta*(lambda - nu_j). (iv) d_j is the first time nu_j(t) reaches lambda; if the curves never cross, the order of the current indices is the order of the first passages. Under a pooled law nu_j(t) = nu(t - e_j) with nu decreasing, so both orders are by turn end e_j, and f'(x) = L*(lambda - nu(a* + x)) is non-decreasing. Counterexample with crossing curves: A has index 5 lambda now and is due in 1 s; B has index 2 lambda and is due in 10 s; each write takes 1 s. Lowest index first finishes B at 1 s and A at 2 s (A is 1 s late); EDD finishes A at 1 s and B at 2 s (nothing late).
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.2 'So writes are jobs with due dates, like reads: write in the order in which pages will be evicted (lowest clean index first), and no later than d_w. With an idle device, write at once (it is free); with a busy device, order all transfers by due date' and 7.3 'writing in eviction order'. Holds under M1 (cost) or as feasibility; among overdue pages it is the lowest-index order (M3). The parenthesis equates two orders that differ when index curves cross: the rule is due-date order. Under LRU-like eviction the engine's FIFO queue is already this order, so candidate change R2 changes nothing unless eviction becomes class-aware. 'It is free' needs sigma = 0 and a write that cannot delay a read arriving during it (one 128-page batch is about 0.38 s of device time).

results.name: R13 When eager writing is optimal; this workload
results.statement: Let kappa_now be the device price when the page is born, kappa_due the expected price when its write would be due, q the probability that the write is ever needed (the host copy is given up while the session is alive), eps the probability that the page is forced out of memory before a deferred write completes, pi the chance of return then, sigma = 0. To first order (ignoring the extra rent of the lazy page), writing at birth is optimal iff kappa_now*L/beta <= q*kappa_due*L/beta + eps*pi*(K_d - K_c). (i) Idle device (kappa_now = 0): eager is weakly optimal. (ii) Constant price, no forced evictions: lazy is weakly optimal and saves the share 1 - q of the write volume. (iii) At saturation K_d - K_c = (mu*gamma - kappa/beta)*L, so with kappa_now = kappa_due = kappa eager wins as soon as eps*pi >= kappa*(1 - q)/(mu*gamma*beta - kappa); mu*gamma*beta = 86 at mu = 93, so the threshold is 0.004 for kappa = 1 and 1 - q = 0.35, and 0.046 for kappa = 10. (iv) For a host time-to-live of d seconds, q = (1 - e)*x/(x + e - x*e) over all pages (x/(x + e - x*e) for pages of a turn that is not the last), x = P(gap > d) per gap, e = probability that a turn is the session's last. (v) With a price that switches between idle and busy, the optimum writes whenever the device is idle and, while it is busy, waits until the due date forces the write.
results.proof: Eager pays kappa_now*L/beta now. Lazy pays kappa_due*L/beta with probability q, and with probability eps the only copy is lost before the write, which costs K_d - K_c more at the return (probability pi). Compare. (i), (ii), (iii) are substitutions; (ii) is R9 (ii). (iv) After each turn the session ends with probability e; otherwise a gap follows, longer than d with probability x (the page is then due), else the session returns and the argument repeats: P = (1 - e)*[x + (1 - x)*P]. (v) is the backward induction with the device state added: in the idle state the write is free, so delaying it gains nothing (R9 ii with w = 0); in the busy state waiting has the option value of an idle moment before the due date.
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.2 'On this workload eager writing is right for live sessions: 56 to 67 % of prompt positions are read back from the SSD, 4.2 to 4.5 times each'. The conclusion stands; the reason does not. The read-back share is q, the fraction of writes ever needed (a deferred write would skip the rest, about a third); '4.2 to 4.5 times each' shows the write is worth making (one write replaces that many recomputes by reads), not that it should be early. Eager is right because device time is nearly free at both ends (idle device at light load; at saturation c is near 0 and therefore kappa, the lateness cost of waiting transfers, is near 0) and because losing an only copy costs 86/kappa writes, so a 0.4 % chance of a forced eviction is enough. At light load on FA3 a write has no value at current prices (recompute at mu = 1 is cheaper than a read); it is an investment for later load.

results.name: R14 Born clean, clean only on a full acknowledgement, and revocation
results.statement: (i) Born clean: if every page of the chain from the resident anchor down to page p is on the SSD and complete, p's restore cost is already K_c, so the value of writing it again is 0 (R9 with K_d replaced by K_c) while the write costs kappa*L_p/beta and holds room while it waits: skip it. (ii) The condition is reachability, not the existence of p's own key: with a lookup that stops at the first missing page, a stored page below a deleted ancestor cannot be read, so it is not clean; the missing ancestors must be written, after which the stored descendants are clean again without being rewritten. (iii) Clean is revocable: if the cleaner deletes p's SSD copy or an ancestor's while the host copy exists, p is an only copy again (restore cost K_d). (iv) Counting a page as clean before the whole write is acknowledged prices an only copy at K_c instead of K_d: its index is understated by K_d/K_c (86/kappa at saturation) and the expected loss per page is (K_d - K_c)*P_pay.
results.proof: Keys are chained: key_j = H(key_{j-1}, tokens of page j), so equal keys mean equal token prefixes, and in a causal model the KV of a position depends only on the tokens up to it; a stored page with the same key can therefore replace the recomputed one. (i) is R9 (i) with equal restore costs: the integral over an empty range is 0. (ii) and (iii) follow from the lookup semantics (hicache_nixl stops at the first missing key) and the definition of clean as 'restore cost K_c'. (iv) is R1 with the wrong K: the page is dropped as soon as (K_c/L)*sup F/tau <= lambda although its true index is K_d/K_c times larger; by R9 (i) the loss is the integral of P_pay between the two costs, at least (K_d - K_c)*P_pay(K_d).
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.2 'A page already on the SSD (same chained key) is clean at birth: a recomputed page is not written again' and 'A page counts as clean only when the SSD has acknowledged the whole write'. Both hold. Add: clean means the whole chain above the page is stored (reachable), and a page stops being clean when the cleaner deletes its copy or an ancestor's; today the tree never learns of deletions, so a host copy can be evicted as clean after its SSD copy is gone.
results.numeric_check: No separate computation: definitions plus R9. The reachability facts are checks S1 and S2 of /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/design_unified_1126/agents/math_retain/ssd_chain.py; the factor 86/kappa is numbers_c34.py item 1 (mu*gamma*beta with mu = 93, gamma = 0.043 ms, beta = 21,400 tokens/s).

results.name: R15 One tier up: the backup GPU to host is a job due at GPU eviction (the mirror)
results.statement: A page is on the GPU until time d_G, when the GPU gives it up (the engine chooses d_G). A host copy made at b <= d_G costs lambda*L*(d_G - b) of rent before d_G and changes no other cost, because every use of the page before d_G is served by the GPU copy. Hence: (i) for lambda > 0 and a copy cost that does not depend on b, the optimal backup time is the latest feasible one, d_G - L/beta_GH (beta_GH = GPU-to-host copy rate); (ii) the index of an existing mirror copy is nu_m = (K_b/L)/(d_G - now - L/beta_GH)^+, where K_b is the priced cost of making the copy at d_G instead; (iii) K_b = 0 if the late copy does not delay the scheduler: then nu_m = 0 and the mirror is first out together with ended sessions; K_b = mu*L/beta_GH if the copy blocks the scheduler: then the eager backup is optimal whenever lambda*(d_G - now) < mu/beta_GH; (iv) GPU eviction itself is R1 with the GPU's price of memory and K = the load time when a host copy exists (K_b when none does).
results.proof: Take any policy and any sample path. Compare it with the same policy in which the host copy of the page is made at d_G - L/beta_GH instead of b. Until d_G every read of the page uses the GPU copy in both; from d_G on the host copy exists in both. TTFT is identical on the path; rent is lower by lambda*L*(d_G - L/beta_GH - b). This gives (i). (ii): dropping the mirror now and copying again at d_G saves lambda*L*(d_G - now - L/beta_GH) of rent and costs K_b; equate. (iii): substitution. (iv): the GPU tier has the same structure (rent on GPU tokens, a restore cost at the next use).
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.1 'the mirror ...: nothing reads it while the GPU holds the page, so its nu is that of the copy being needed after the GPU gives the page up', 4.3 'GPU to host: the backup is due when the GPU gives the page up. Write-through makes it at the end of prefill, so the mirror holds 0.65 M of 1.63 M host tokens for nothing ... dropping mirror copies once their SSD write is acknowledged, or backing up at GPU eviction, pays lambda only when it buys something', and 'The same index orders GPU eviction'. Holds in the priced model if the late backup is asynchronous. The bullet should state the index, (cost of a late backup)/(L x time to GPU eviction). 'For nothing' is false if the backup at GPU eviction runs inline, as the existing write_back path does: at mu = 93 one blocked copy of a 24.9 K history costs 6.6 TTFT-seconds, more than its rent over an 8 s decode for any lambda below 3e-5. Dropping the mirror after the SSD acknowledgement and copying again at the turn's end makes two copies per turn; one backup at the turn's end, issued like today's end-of-prefill copies, makes one.
results.numeric_check: numbers_c34.py item 4 (arithmetic on the brief's constants; nothing measured here): mirror 0.65 M of 1.63 M tokens; without it the host-only room grows from 0.92 M by a factor 1.71; the mirror's rent is 0.15 s per request at lambda = 5e-7, 0.59 s at 2e-6 (2.2 requests/s); a copy of 24,900 tokens takes about 70 ms at the one measured rate (2,304 tokens in 6.5 ms), 0.15 of one copy stream at 2.2 requests/s; if it blocked the scheduler it would cost mu*L/beta_GH = 6.6 TTFT-seconds per request, i.e. nu_m = 2.6e-4/(seconds to GPU eviction) per token against lambda of order 1e-6.

results.name: R16 One tier down: SSD capacity with chained pages (tail before head; the index of a shared head)
results.statement: Lookup: it starts just below the session's resident anchor (the deepest page still in GPU or host memory) and reads stored pages down the chain until the first missing one. (i) One chain, pages i < j, lookups with no resident anchor inside [i, j): if page i is deleted and page j kept, deleting j and keeping i instead retrieves at least as much on every lookup. For lookups from the root, among all ways to delete m pages of a chain of n the tail is the unique optimum and loses exactly m pages. (ii) With anchors between i and j the exchange can fail: deleting page j from a full chain loses P(anchor above j)*(n - j + 1) pages per lookup, which is smallest at the head when the head is usually resident. (iii) Tree of page groups v (size len_v), root-anchored lookups, session s with lookup rate rho_s, theta = mu*gamma - (c + kappa)/beta the value per token read instead of recomputed: for every SSD price sigma per token-second the optimal stored set is {v : theta*rho(v) > sigma}, rho(v) = sum of rho_s over the sessions whose chain passes through v. The sets are nested in sigma, so deleting in increasing theta*rho(v) is optimal for every capacity equal to a threshold set's size (and for the divisible problem in between); rho does not rise down a chain, so a tail goes no later than its head; an ended session contributes 0. With time-varying return laws rho_s is replaced by the session's hazard of a cold return, and the hazards of independent sessions add. (iv) Shared head h that is sometimes resident: with rho_s^cold the rate of lookups of s that find h not resident and n_s the stored tokens of s below h, the SSD copy of h is worth theta*sum_s rho_s^cold*(len_h + n_s) per second, an index theta*sum_s rho_s^cold*(1 + n_s/len_h) per token; it is 0 if h is never cold.
results.proof: (i) A lookup whose anchor is at or below j needs neither page. A lookup whose anchor is above i stops, when i is deleted, at or before page i - 1; after the swap the pages before i are unchanged and i is present, so it reads at least as far. Uniqueness: a deleted set D with m pages has min D <= n - m + 1; a root lookup loses n - min D + 1 >= m pages, with equality iff D is the last m pages. (ii) A lookup with its anchor above j, on a chain complete except for j, loses pages j to n. (iii) For root-anchored lookups a page below a missing ancestor is never read, so the stored set may be taken ancestor-closed without loss; then value(S) - sigma*size(S) = sum over v in S of len_v*(theta*rho(v) - sigma). Every lookup through a child passes through its parent, so rho does not rise down a chain and {theta*rho > sigma} is ancestor-closed; it maximises the sum term by term. A set that maximises value - sigma*size is optimal among all sets of at most its size (Everett 1963). (iv) Lookups of s start at the root at rate rho_s^cold (they need h and then the chain) and below h otherwise (they do not use h's SSD copy); the difference of values with and without h on the SSD is the stated sum.
results.draft_claim_checked: 4.3 'SSD capacity: the cleaner is eviction on the SSD, by the same index with K = K_rec for the whole chain below a page: ended sessions' chains first, a chain's tail before its head (a lookup stops at the first missing page), a head shared by live sessions last'. Proved for lookups that start above the pages concerned. Changes: the head's index is a sum of rates over the sessions below it, with each session's stake the head plus its stored chain, not one K_rec; 'a shared head last' is wrong for a head that is always resident, whose SSD copy is worth nothing: the cleaner may delete it before any tail, provided the cache then treats the host copy as an only copy (R14 iii); 'ended sessions' chains first' applies to the part no live session shares.

S2: chain of 8 pages, one page to delete: lookups from the root: loss 8, 7, ..., 1 by deleted page (delete the tail); anchor uniform: 1.00 at both ends, up to 2.50 in the middle; head usually resident (root lookups 2 %): deleting page 4 loses 0.10 against 1.00 for the tail. improvements: Hull theorem as the paper's Retain statement. Plot each hint law as the curve (E[min(G,t)], P(G>t)). Its lower convex hull is the session's efficient frontier of memory-time against restore probability; the index is the hull's slope (R3). Sketch of use: (a) one O(n) pass over the engine's 64 support points gives nu at every age; (b) the drop age at price lambda is a tangency, so each session has a demand curve x_i(lambda) = I_i(s_i(lambda)); (c) the price that clears a room R solves sum_i rate_i L_i x_i(lambda) = R, a closed form for section 6 in place of a learned price; (d) Belady, LRU and 'keep to the return or not at all' are the point, convex and concave cases of the same picture.

One index for every host holder: nu = (K0/L)/(g + W - rho)^+, K0 the price-free restore cost, g = inf_h tau/F the Gittins holding time (0 for a queued turn, R0 for an exact hint, 1/hazard for falling hazards, infinite for an ended session), W the queue wait, rho the restore's own hold (R7, verified on 4,000 random cases). The mirror fits too (g = time to GPU eviction, K0 = cost of a late backup, R15). This would replace 4.1's separate bullets and 5.1's class order by one ranking 'time to next GPU use net of the restore's own hold'. Corollary worth stating: a long queue flattens the value of hints. On the tool law g is 2.6 s at age 0 and 11.9 s at age 10 s; with no queue the index differs by 4.6x between those sessions, with W = 20 s by (11.9 + 20)/(2.6 + 20) = 1.41x. Only human-gap sessions (g of 100 s and more) stay clearly separated, which matches the measured ties of the hinted arms under saturation.

A provable ceiling on what hints can buy for retention. The priced bound of R6 (weak duality over the hull curves) is a lower bound on the miss ratio of every non-anticipative policy with a given information level. In the equal-size toy with the trace's two gap entries and room for 25 % of the sessions: no class information 0.0936 (LRU reaches 0.0954 at 512 to 2,048 sessions, the time-to-live approximation), class known 0.0734 (the index policy reaches 0.0749 to 0.0754), exact gaps 0.0445 (clairvoyant order). At 50 %: 0.0344, 0.0325, 0.0151. Sketch: compute the same three bounds from the replayed gaps of a campaign and report measured SSD-read shares against them; the paper can then say how much of the gap between LRU and the oracle a distribution hint can close at all (about 22 % of misses at a quarter of the sessions held, 6 % at half).

The write's life in two theorems (R9, R10): (1) at a constant device price a write is never better early than late, so the write-back point is the eviction frontier; (2) a dirty page has exactly two candidate lives, chosen by V0(K_rec) - V0(K_read + w) >= w P(ended), with the pointwise threshold P(return) > w/(K_rec - K_read). Add the closed form for the share of pages ever due under a host stay d: q = (1 - e) x/(x + e - x e), x = P(gap > d), e = P(a turn is the last). It gives 57 to 74 % for 30 to 60 s against the measured 56 to 67 % read back, and predicts that a deferred write would skip 26 to 43 % of the write volume (about 1.1 to 1.8 K of 4.3 K tokens/s). An offline count of written pages never read back, by class, would test this prediction on the campaign 34 logs.

A copy-down rule that explains both the eager SSD write and the wasted mirror. For a copy from tier X to the tier below: earliness costs (price of the lower tier's space) x tokens per second plus the chance the copy turns out unneeded times the transfer price; lateness costs the upper tier's blocked room or the loss of the only copy. With a known due date the copy is made as late as possible when the lower tier's space or the transfer has a price, and at once when both are free. SSD: space free until the volume fills and device nearly free, so eager is optimal. Host: space priced at lambda, so the end-of-prefill backup is the one place the engine pays rent for nothing (0.65 M tokens), unless the late copy would block the scheduler (R15). Sketch of proof: the sample-path argument of R15 plus R9 (ii); with an uncertain due date it becomes the same quantile rule as Fetch (land the copy at the lambda-versus-lateness critical ratio of the due date).

Write priority is the eviction order with the size cancelling. The cost rate of a late write is L_p (lambda - nu_clean) and its device time is L_p/beta, so its Smith ratio is beta (lambda - nu_clean): pages are written lowest clean index first whatever their size, and a late write goes before a late read of L_read tokens iff (lambda - nu_clean) L_read > c (R11, R12). This turns 5.2's comparison into one inequality and shows that the 50 K / 25 K hold is the special case nu_clean = 0. For the cost-optimality of due-date order the exact model is equal-size pages with one convex lateness shape (exchange proof); with returns that cancel a write the oldest-first order was optimal in all 300 small instances, and a coupling proof (older page: higher cost rate and lower chance to leave by itself) looks reachable.

SSD index and the hot-head exception (R16). With root-anchored lookups the index of a page group is theta times the summed cold-return hazard of the sessions below it, so tails-before-heads and ended-sessions-first are corollaries of one monotone quantity, and the cleaner needs only per-page session counts and hazards. A head that is always resident has index 0 on the SSD. If the cleaner reports deletions and the tree marks the host copy as an only copy again, the SSD copy of a hot head can be deleted first and rewritten once when the head cools (cost kappa len_h/beta), which is the opposite of 'refresh heads when memory serves them' (R4 in section 9) and cheaper when the volume is tight. A replay of campaign 34's 48 head-missing requests under both orders would decide between them.

Closed-form index for lognormal hints, and what it says about the hint law. The hazard of a lognormal peaks at exp(m + s z*), z* the root of phi(z)/Phibar(z) = z + s (median x 0.049 for s = 1.79, x 1.76 for s = 0.5); past the peak the index is the hazard, before it the hazard at a tangent point with a one-line equation (R4, agreement with quadrature to 6 or 7 digits). Two consequences for the engine's two-piece form: no lognormal hint has a falling hazard at age 0, so any myopic keep rule evicts at the turn's end (cost 1.98 against 0.73 in the tool-entry example); and the density jumps at the median by sigma_low/sigma_high, upward by 1.44 for the human entry, which makes the index bulge between 74 and 96 s. A single-sigma fit or a smooth splice would remove the artifact. For Pareto-like tails the keep time is linear in the restore cost per token: a* = alpha K/(lambda L) - theta.

Calibrating lambda from the eviction frontier. For one pooled falling-hazard law, lambda = (K0/L) x hazard(T_C)/(1 - rho x hazard(T_C)), T_C the idle age of the pages being evicted. With the trace's gap mix the pooled hazard is 0.022/s at 30 s and 0.0099/s at 60 s, so lambda is about 9e-7 to 4e-7 TTFT-seconds per token-second at light load (K/L = gamma) and about the same times kappa for clean pages at saturation; an only copy at mu = 93 has index 9e-5 to 4e-5 at those ages. Campaign 26's measured value of room (0.52 s per turn for 305 K tokens at 1.1 to 1.5 turns/s) is about 2e-6 on Triton, the same order. The engine's 5e-5 is two orders higher: under the index rule it would keep no clean 25 K prefix even at the turn's end. These are inferred values (numbers_c34.py), to be checked against logged eviction ages.

Size lemma with an exposed fixed read lag. K_read(l) = c (V + lags + l/beta - W)^+ + kappa l/beta for the evicted tail of l tokens is concave in l with a fixed part, so (a) the per-token index of a whole prefix falls with its length (at light load a 2 K prefix has 6x the per-token index of a 25 K one: 5.0e-4 against 8.3e-5), (b) freeing m tokens from one prefix is cheaper than m/2 from each of two by exactly one fixed lag times P(return), (c) at c = 0, or when recompute is the cheaper restore (idle FA3 GPU), the index is size-neutral. This is the GreedyDual-Size effect derived from the cost model instead of assumed, and it says leaf-first eviction should finish one session's chain before starting another's when stalls are exposed.

Open item worth a proof or a counterexample: indexability with early re-fetch (the keep set was an interval in the price in all 15 cases of refetch.py, R8), and finite-N optimality of LRU under one pooled falling-hazard law with equal sizes and costs (the simulation shows only convergence to the priced bound). Both would let section 7 claim more than the relaxed-problem optimum.
